verdicts.notes:
I checked all 11 cards in section 2.1 (5 true, 6 false). Average statement length is 102.6 for true cards and 101.3 for false ones. Hedge words are spread across both answers ("can" appears in 2 true and 2 false cards). Every source URL loads, is on learn.microsoft.com and is current. Key quotes:
- 01: storage-network-security-limitations says "Azure Storage firewall rules apply only to data plane operations. Control plane operations aren't subject to the restrictions specified in firewall rules."
- 02: storage-network-security says "The virtual network can be from any subscription within any Microsoft Entra tenant across any Azure region."
- 03, 04, 05: the correct azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview page says "A user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key". It also says the account SAS can delegate "Service-level operations (For example, the Get/Set Service Properties ...)" and that "Stored access policies are not supported for the user delegation SAS or the account SAS."
- 06: storage-account-keys-manage says "rotating or regenerating access keys revokes shared access signatures (SAS) that are generated based on that key."
- 07: the same page says "Having two keys ensures that your application maintains access to Azure Storage throughout the process", and its rotation steps move clients to the secondary key first.
- 08: storage-files-active-directory-overview says "You can use only one identity source for file access authentication per storage account, and it applies to all file shares in the account." Managed identity can coexist on the same account, but it is not one of the three identity sources, so the answer holds.
- 09: storage-files-active-directory-overview says "the identity needs share-level permission and the appropriate file or directory permission." The authorization overview says a share-level permission grants "access to the share only and nothing else, not even the root directory."
- 11: storage-files-identity-configure-file-level-permissions says "When you mount a share with a storage account key, you get immediate full access to all files and directories", in contrast with the SMB Admin role, where "the existing ACLs still apply".

Borderline cards I did not flag:
- 07 is close to a truism: the whole point of having two keys is that rotation keeps access. It is still Azure-specific and in the exam's style.
- 09: the explanation says a share-level grant alone gives no file access, which matches the documentation. In practice, though, the default root ACL gives Authenticated Users Modify, so a share-level role alone often works on a fresh share. A rewrite could say the ACL check still applies.
- 06: the wording "key-signed SAS" is awkward but unambiguous. Revoking user delegation keys also invalidates those tokens, so the answer stays false under either reading.

No duplicates with other sections. The closest card is s1.2-02 (Reader cannot list keys), which tests a different fact. Nothing in this section is retired or in preview, and no statement relies on the old storage-sas-overview URL that the prompt warns about.

flagged.evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/object-replication-overview: "After you create the replication policy, write operations to the destination container aren't permitted. Any attempts to write to the destination container fail with error code 409 (Conflict)." The same page also says: "Read and delete operations to the destination container are permitted when the replication policy is active." and "You can call the Set Blob Tier operation on a blob in the destination container to move it to the archive tier."
flagged.problem: The statement says "modify blobs". Deleting a blob and changing its tier with Set Blob Tier both count as modifying it, and both are permitted on an active destination container. An expert could therefore answer True. The explanation is also too broad when it says the container rejects client writes in general, because deletes and tier changes still succeed.
flagged.suggestedFix: Answer stays false. Statement: "An application can upload new blobs to an object replication destination container while its rule is active." Explanation: "While a replication rule is active, writes to its destination container fail with 409 (Conflict); reads and deletes still work. Remove the rule or policy before writing there." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/access-tiers-overview: "To change the redundancy configuration for a storage account that contains blobs in the archive tier, you must first rehydrate all archived blobs to the hot, cool, or cold tier." The same page then gives an exception: "Migrating a storage account from LRS to GRS is supported as long as no blobs were moved to the archive tier while the account was configured for LRS." https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/redundancy-migration: "To convert an LRS, GRS or RA-GRS account to one that supports zone-redundancy, first move the archived blobs to a storage account that supports blobs in the archive tier." Footnote 2 of the same page flags archive only for changes "to geo- or zone-redundant". https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-redundancy-change-faq: "You can also delete any archived data before converting."
flagged.problem: The card makes a blanket claim that rehydration comes before any redundancy change, and it closely paraphrases the source sentence. Official pages list exceptions and alternatives: LRS to GRS is allowed when the blobs were archived while the account was GRS, removing geo-redundancy is not listed as blocked, and archived blobs can be moved to another account or deleted instead of rehydrated. An expert could argue that the general claim is false.
flagged.suggestedFix: Answer stays true. Statement: "An LRS account holding archived blobs needs them rehydrated or removed before Azure converts it to ZRS." Explanation: "ZRS doesn't support the archive tier, so archived blobs must be rehydrated to hot, cool or cold, moved to another account or deleted before the conversion; a manual migration is the alternative." URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/redundancy-migration

rewrite.reason: explanation_error: the claim that an assigned group mixes users and devices is not on the cited page. Statement kept, explanation replaced with the page's member-type facts.
rewrite.statement: Administrators can add device objects as members of Microsoft Entra ID security groups.
rewrite.explanation: Security groups accept users, devices and service principals as members, while Microsoft 365 groups accept only users, so device targeting relies on security groups.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Learn About Groups, Group Membership, and Access - Microsoft Entra

rewrite.reason: weak_card (hedge truism, and the 'scheduling' clause is unsupported). Dropping 02, 10 and 11 would leave 8 cards, so this one is replaced with the verifier's suggestion, confirmed on view-recommendations: 'Configuration settings apply to the subscription or resource group, so the same settings apply to everyone that has access'.
rewrite.statement: Excluding a resource group in Azure Advisor configuration also hides its recommendations from other users with access.
rewrite.explanation: Advisor configuration settings belong to the subscription or resource group, not to the viewer, so the same exclusion applies to everyone who has access to that scope.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Configure Azure Advisor recommendations view

rewrite.reason: explanation_error plus better source: Kerberos is allowed by default. files-smb-protocol says 'By default, all authentication methods are allowed. Kerberos must be enabled to use identity-based authentication' and 'NTLMv2 (storage account key only)'. Statement kept.
rewrite.statement: Azure Files identity-based SMB access requires Kerberos in the account's SMB authentication settings.
rewrite.explanation: Kerberos is allowed by default in the SMB security settings. If a custom profile removes it, identity-based mounts fail, because Azure Files accepts NTLMv2 only with the storage account key.
rewrite.sourceTitle: SMB File Shares in Azure Files

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the blanket 'any redundancy change' claim has documented exceptions. Narrowed to LRS to ZRS. redundancy-migration says 'ZRS, GZRS and RA-GZRS storage accounts don't support the archive tier... first move the archived blobs to a storage account that supports blobs in the archive tier', and manual migration applies when 'rehydrating the data isn't desired'.
rewrite.statement: An administrator rehydrates or moves out an LRS account's archived blobs before converting the account to ZRS.
rewrite.explanation: ZRS, GZRS and RA-GZRS accounts don't support the archive tier, so archived blobs return to an online tier or move to another account first; a manual migration is the alternative.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Change how a storage account is replicated

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'modify' covered delete and Set Blob Tier, which are permitted. Narrowed to uploads (writes). Page: 'write operations to the destination container aren't permitted... fail with error code 409 (Conflict)'; 'Read and delete operations... are permitted'.
rewrite.statement: An application can upload new blobs to an object replication destination container while its policy is active.
rewrite.explanation: While a replication policy is active, writes to its destination container fail with 409 (Conflict); reads and deletes still work. Remove the rule or policy before writing there.
rewrite.misconception: An object replication destination container accepts new uploads from client applications.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Object replication overview

rewrite.reason: weak_card (hedge truism). 2.2 needs two of its four weak or out-of-scope cards rewritten to keep 9 cards, and this is the only encryption card. rewrite.statement: An administrator who configures customer-managed keys at storage account creation uses a user-assigned managed identity.
rewrite.explanation: At account creation, Key Vault access for customer-managed keys uses a user-assigned managed identity; on an existing account either a user-assigned or a system-assigned identity works.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Customer-managed keys for account encryption

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman on a 2019 page). This is the second required 2.2 rewrite and the only Storage Explorer card. It also places 'requires' on a false card, against the scan's top tell. Current page: Storage Explorer connects either by signing in to Azure or by attaching an individual resource, and it 'can connect to the following resource types using a SAS URI: Blob container... File share, Queue, Table' with no sign-in step.
rewrite.statement: Azure Storage Explorer requires an Azure account sign-in before it attaches a blob container by its SAS URL.

- 1.3: 10 rewritten (Advisor configuration scope); 02 and 11 dropped.
- 2.2: 08 (customer-managed keys) and 10 (Storage Explorer) rewritten to keep encryption and tool coverage; 02 and 03 dropped. 04 and 06 rewritten as ambiguous.
- 2.3: 07 rewritten (metadata update creates a version); 03 dropped.

- 3.1-08 keeps volatility may_change (what-if evaluation keeps evolving). 2.2-08 should be difficulty 3; 3.3-06 and 4.2-09 difficulty 2.
